Over the past decade, United States President Donald Trump has become a figurehead for right-wing populist movements around the world.

From Europe to Asia, politicians have borrowed from his playbook, attacking institutions and the media, courting controversy and mobilising voter grievances over immigration, national identity and culture war issues.

But with the Republican Party suffering a crushing defeat in this month's US midterm elections, questions are emerging about whether Trump's political appeal is waning — and what that could mean for Trump-inspired politicians in Australia and around the world.

David Smith, associate professor of American politics and foreign policy at the United States Studies Centre, tells SBS News: "Trump has really, for the last 10 years, been an icon of the global far-right, and there have been politicians all over the world, including in Australia, who have really modelled themselves on Trump and have really tried to follow his style of politics wherever they can."

He argues the scale of the Republican defeat suggests growing voter fatigue with Trump's style of politics, particularly when expectations around economic performance and governing are not met. He says the result could serve as a warning to politicians elsewhere who have adopted a similar approach.

They elected Trump to bring prices down. They elected him to actually do something for them in government. They didn't elect Trump because they just wanted to see endless more iterations of the Trump show.
The US result comes amid a broader series of electoral setbacks for right-wing and populist parties in several countries, including Serbia, Brazil, Hungary and Israel.

However, these outcomes have unfolded in different political and economic circumstances, making it difficult to establish a common trend or attribute the results to a broader rejection of right-wing populism.
In some cases, dissatisfaction with incumbent governments over economic uncertainty and frustration over rising living costs may be a significant factor.

Jordan McSwiney, a senior research fellow at the University of Canberra's Centre for Deliberative Democracy, cautions against interpreting these electoral losses as evidence of a global rejection of far-right politics.
"The biggest thread between them is, in basically every case except Brazil, there's an incumbency effect," he tells SBS News.
I don't think it means that we've reached some kind of inflection point where voters around the world are saying no to these politics.
"Because there are other places where the far-right is looking like they may very well perform very well at the next set of elections, including Australia."
One Nation's Trump problem
In the wake of the US midterm elections, eagle-eyed observers noted that a blog post on One Nation's website comparing the party's policies and political approach with those of Trump was removed.

"Want Trump's action and style, then it's One Nation you need," read the post, originally published on 23 January 2025, three days after Trump's second presidential inauguration, according to online archives.

It included a graphic depicting party leader Pauline Hanson alongside Trump and outlined areas of policy alignment between the two, including immigration, energy, national sovereignty and cultural issues. The post described One Nation as the only party in Australia that mirrored Trump's priorities.
The post has since disappeared from One Nation's website, although it is unclear when or why it was removed.

Polling earlier this year from the Australian Financial Review/Redbridge/Accent Research found Hanson's support for Trump was the biggest deterrent among voters considering or already supporting One Nation.

Hanson has been a vocal supporter of Trump, and travelled to Florida to speak at the Conservative Political Action Conference hosted at his luxury Mar-a-Lago resort last year. Her support for the US war in Iran has also put her at odds with some European far-right leaders.

Political science professor Duncan McDonnell, who researches the populist radical right at Flinders University, tells SBS News "there might be a price to be paid" for Hanson's close association with Trump.

Referring to Peter Dutton's 2025 election loss, McDonnell says the former Liberal leader was "very much leaning into this sort of Australian version of MAGA, and it didn't play well at all with voters".
McSwiney cautions against viewing One Nation's political identity solely through its association with Trump, pointing to Hanson's long-standing positions on immigration and national identity.
He says the party's growing popularity in Australia is more closely related to domestic economic pressures and dissatisfaction with the major parties.
Hanson was doing Trump before Trump, right? She was doing all of this stuff since 1996.
"And also it's not the first time that Trump's lost his lustre or an election."
The big lesson, McSwiney says, is that voters are clearly very concerned about the cost of living, and "incumbent governments are getting hammered around the world".
In Victoria, where One Nation has historically struggled to make electoral inroads, the party is attracting stronger support ahead of this month's state election.

While McSwiney doesn't expect the Republican Party's midterm defeat to have a comparable effect on One Nation in Australia, he says the party may now distance itself from the Trump brand to some extent.

"I think the big thing is that it's kind of just a bit embarrassing. I mean, the Republicans got flogged. One Nation wants to look and present itself like a winner, so they probably don't want to talk too much about their similarities to losers," he says.
One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce attributed the Republican setback, in part, to Trump developing a "grandiose" view of himself in the lead-up to the elections.

"The general path of leaders, even in Australia, is prime minister. Then they believe they're president. Then they believe they're king. And then the next thing they are infallible, and they're with the pope, and then they're voted out," he said in an interview with News24 earlier this month.
"And I think that, unfortunately, President Trump, as much as I respect the process of democracy in the United States, became a little bit too much focused on President Trump."
SBS News has contacted One Nation for comment but did not receive a response before publication.
Trump and the global far right

While many far-right leaders share Trump's position on immigration and culture war issues, his criticism of traditional allies, opposition to NATO, threats against Greenland and shifting tariff policies have complicated his relationships with allies.
McDonnell says Trump has been a somewhat "embarrassing friend" for some European far-right leaders.
"Any kind of association with him now, I think, is becoming something of a liability for a lot of right-wing populists," he says.
"It's a kind of balancing act that I think a lot of [them] have to perform."
The changing public perception of Trump has been reflected in international polling.

A Pew Research Center survey earlier this year found broadly negative views of the US president across many countries, with confidence in his leadership declining even among supporters of right-wing populist parties in some European nations.
In the days following the midterm elections, several European far-right politicians commented on the Republican defeat and its implications for Trump's foreign policy.

Alice Weidel, one of the leaders of the far-right Alternative for Germany party, said after the vote earlier this month that Trump's "broken promise" to keep the US out of foreign wars had "come back to haunt the Republicans".
In Spain, the leader of the far-right party Vox, Santiago Abascal, told reporters the day after the elections he was "in Spain and not in Michigan".
"I care quite little about what happens in other places," said the politician, who attended Trump's inauguration last year and has previously described him as a "comrade-in-arms".
Leaders in France and Italy also linked the outcome to dissatisfaction with the US role in the war in the Middle East.
The impact of the Republican defeat on Trump's international counterparts remains unclear, with upcoming European elections set to provide further insight.

Spain will vote at the end of November, and Vox — which previously campaigned to 'Make Spain Great Again' — could become the first far-right party to enter Spanish national government since the country's return to democracy.
Italy's right-wing Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni also faces an election next year as she seeks a second term.

Meloni, who had a public falling-out with Trump on social media in June, struck a diplomatic tone after the midterms, saying she would not typically comment on US domestic politics. But her deputy, foreign minister Antonio Tajani, told Italian newspaper Il Messaggero on 4 November that neither he nor Meloni were followers of Trump's MAGA movement.
And in France, far-right candidate Marine Le Pen remains a prominent contender ahead of next year's presidential election, despite an embezzlement conviction.

McSwiney points to electoral gains by populist right-wing movements in other parts of the world, including Germany's Saxony-Anhalt, the United Kingdom's local elections, and Colombia's presidential vote — as well as One Nation's Farrer by-election win earlier this year.
He says these developments suggest these movements' electoral fortunes remain mixed across countries.
